analysis.one_liner: Stops employers from cutting workers' health insurance during strikes or lockouts.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate committee where it was assigned, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to make it an unlawful labor practice for an employer to terminate or change an employee's group health plan coverage while locking workers out or while employees are on a lawful strike. It would add civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation for lockouts and $50,000 for strikes, doubled in repeat cases, and allow penalties against directors or officers who directed or tolerated the violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking and locked-out workers and their families, who today can lose employer health coverage mid-strike — an employer pressure tactic that leaves them without insurance at the exact moment they have no paycheck.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Striking and locked-out workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act for an employer to terminate or alter an employee's group health plan coverage during a lockout or a lawful strike [S2][S3].

Adds civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation for coverage cut during a lockout and up to $50,000 for a strike, doubled to $150,000 and $100,000 where the employer has violated the same rule within five years or where serious economic harm results [S3].

Allows the labor board to assess penalties directly against directors or officers who directed the violation, had authority to prevent it and failed to, or knew of it, so executives can be personally liable [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially large companies facing strikes or lockouts, who would lose a bargaining tactic — cutting off health coverage to raise pressure on workers — and would face new civil penalties, including possible personal liability for executives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers facing strikes or lockouts

drawbacks.text: Employers would lose one lawful form of economic pressure in collective bargaining and would bear new civil penalties, which business groups argue raises the cost of employment disputes; the bill would also apply retroactively-defined obligations to plans employers currently fund.

Coverage disputes could grow more expensive for mid-sized employers: penalties are assessed per violation, with doubling for repeat conduct, and the bill permits board judgments on company size and public interest, so outcomes depend heavily on agency discretion.
The bill only protects coverage during a strike or lockout itself; it does not address wages, pension, or other bargaining issues, so its scope is narrow relative to the wider dispute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and narrow: workers who walk a picket line or are locked out keep their family's health insurance, which is one of the highest-stakes things a strike currently puts at risk. The cost falls on employers who lose one pressure tactic and face penalties of $50,000-$150,000 per violation — significant for small employers, modest for large corporations. The bill does not change wages or other bargaining outcomes, so its effect on labor disputes overall is limited, but for affected workers and their families it removes the risk of catastrophic coverage loss during the dispute.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 8, 2023 by Sen. Sherrod Brown along with 12 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action is recorded — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and any bill not passed by both chambers dies with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers retain the ability to cut health coverage during strikes and lockouts without new penalties; the bill's 13 Senate supporters never got a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who keep the coverage-cutting tactic

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 cosponsors from his caucus.

for.name: Bob Casey, Bernie Sanders, Tammy Baldwin, Richard Blumenthal, John Fetterman, Ed Markey, Alex Padilla, Tina Smith, Chris Van Hollen, Elizabeth Warren, Sheldon Whitehouse, Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all Democratic caucus members, none from the Republican conference.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (majority Democratic at the time), chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — for the remaining 22 months of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored or supported the bill; with the Democratic majority not advancing it, no path to floor action existed.

against.name: Employer and business groups
against.what_they_did: Oppose proposals extending strike protections and NLRB penalties on employers generally; while the record does not show specific action on this bill, such groups are the affected industry interest in keeping the coverage-cutting tactic available.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 Senate supporters were Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill; it also never advanced within the Democratic-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Large employers and employers facing unionization or strikes
industries.note: The bill takes away one bargaining tactic — terminating or altering health coverage during a lockout or strike — and adds civil penalties up to $150,000 per violation, with possible personal liability for executives. That tactic's cost falls directly on workers and their families, who can lose insurance mid-dispute.

industries.industry: Group health insurers and employer health plan administrators
industries.note: Employer plans would simply keep running during disputes rather than being terminated, so insurers keep premiums flowing; the mechanism barely changes their role or revenue.
